newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW-Asian stocks to gain from Hong Kong flows.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Asian stocks to gain from Hong Kong flows.

text.p: Rumours that investors are switching out of Hong Kong stocks and into regional markets are starting to filter through Hong Kong's investment community, but the movements have yet to take concrete form.

With Hong Kong stocks falling after reaching an all-time high last Tuesday, some market players are convinced the time is right to take profits on Asian-dedicated funds and seek higher returns elsewhere in the region.

The Hang Seng index closed at a record 13,868.24 points on January 20 after hitting an intra-session high of 13,994.86. But on Friday, the blue-chip index followed New York stocks lower, shedding 230 points to close 1.17 percent weaker at 13,379.
Despite the sell-off, regional traders told Reuters they had yet to detect any tangible switching to other markets.
"Everyone's talking about it, but I haven't seen it," said one regional trader at a big Hong Kong investment house.
Four regional traders contacted on Friday all denied seeing or participating in regional switching.
But asset managers, always reluctant to admit their current activities, were divided.

Jardine Fleming Unit Trusts investment director Patrick Wong said Hong Kong still offered value, thanks to rising confidence about its return to China on July 1, and stocks were trading at an average price-to-earnings ratio of 13.5.
A fairer valuation would be 17 times earnings, which should push the Hang Seng index to at least 15,500 before investors started to reassess their portfolios, he said.
"I don't see any immediate outflow of funds to other parts of Asia given that other Southeast Asian markets are not really as attractive as Hong Kong from a lot of angles," Wong added.
Jardine Fleming, one of Hong Kong's largest mutual fund companies, said it remained heavily overweight on Hong Kong with a nearly 50-percent ratio in its Asian ex-Japan model portfolio.

But another leading asset manager, who declined to be named, said it had joined a number of other investors locking in Hong Kong profits at current levels, particularly in China-related stocks such as red chips and H shares.
Red chips are Hong Kong-controlled companies that derive most of their earnings from China. H shares are China state enterprises listed in Hong Kong.
"They tend to be the ones that have run up the most. Red chips are trading in the 20s. You've got to be cautious about those," the asset manager said.
Hongkong Bank also fell prey to profit-taking, he said. It closed HK$2.50 weaker on Friday at HK$177.50, down from a high of HK$183 on January 17.
Favoured beneficiaries of the allocation changes were Indonesia, Singapore, the Philippines and possibly Thailand or South Korea.
"Indonesia is the place most people are looking at," the fund manager said. "Interest rates are coming down, and that will be beneficial for asset prices."
The Philippines was also expected to benefit following news of a possible sovereign debt rating upgrade by Moody's Investors Service Inc and further earnings momentum.

Opinion remained divided on South Korea, seen as continuing to suffer from poor economic fundamentals, while some asset managers said they were moving into Thailand in anticipation of a mid-year recovery.
